abstract: -Linolenic acid (ALA) is a dietary precursor of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) but estimates of its conversion to DHA generally rely on circulating measurements rather than brain DHA turnover. We investigated whether increasing dietary chia oil-derived ALA supports brain DHA concentrations and turnover compared with preformed DHA from fish oil. Male C57BL/6J mice received diets containing 0.2%, 0.9%, 1.8%, 4.5%, or 9% ALA, or a reference diet containing 1.8% ALA and 0.9% DHA, expressed as percentages of total dietary fat. After six weeks, mice were switched to corresponding diets enriched with uniformly carbon-13-labelled ALA or, for the reference group, labelled DHA. Mice were euthanized over 168 days; DHA concentrations and carbon isotope signatures were measured in plasma, liver, and brain to estimate DHA turnover. Brain DHA concentrations in the 1.8%, 4.5%, and 9% ALA groups were not significantly different from the reference group at any time point. At 9% ALA, DHA half-lives were 15.7, 11.7, and 70.6 days in plasma, liver, and brain, respectively, versus 15.1, 7.2, and 55.4 days in the reference group. Estimated DHA loss rates reached 78%, 51%, and 76% of reference values, respectively, despite estimated dietary ALA conversion to plasma DHA remaining below 0.5%. Higher dietary ALA intakes supported brain DHA concentrations and turnover, suggesting that ALA-derived DHA may contribute to brain DHA maintenance when preformed DHA intake is limited.
